title: API Release Readiness
learning_outcomes: Explain how api release readiness affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from functional and contract tests to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on api release readiness in api governance, teamwork, and professional practices. You will connect functional and contract tests to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: API Release Readiness matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying functional and contract tests deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Lesson 239 concept map
content_blocks.alt_text: Lesson 239: Functional and contract tests → Security and performance checks → Documentation and operational readiness → Release criteria and rollback planning.
content_blocks.caption: Follow the 4 syllabus topics in order, then inspect the example.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Professional API work includes shared standards, clear ownership, decision records, change review, lifecycle planning, and operational cost. In this lesson, treat “API Release Readiness” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: API Release Readiness
content_blocks.code:
decision: choose_cursor_pagination
context: collection_size_is_growing
options:
  - offset_limit
  - cursor_based
choice: cursor_based
consequences:
  - stable_ordering_is_required
  - cursor_tokens_are_validated_and_opaque
  - clients_need_continuation_handling
content_blocks.expected_output: A short decision record identifies context, alternatives, choice, and consequences so future maintainers can review the trade-off.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Functional and contract tests”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Security and performance checks” and “Release criteria and rollback planning”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Write down important decisions and make ownership, quality gates, and retirement criteria explicit. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating api release readiness. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “Functional and contract tests” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for API Release Readiness with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating api release readiness as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: Professional API work includes shared standards, clear ownership, decision records, change review, lifecycle planning, and operational cost. In this lesson, treat “API Release Readiness” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.
Next, connect this idea to Lesson 240: Professional API Engineering Review.
